title: `randomized_smiles` is one-hot encoded against a vocabulary and a maximum length measured on CANONICAL SMILES
what_the_code_does: `generate_aggregate_stats` builds the token vocabulary and `max_sequence_length` by tokenizing `smiles_data.canonical_smiles`, even when the requested representation is `randomized_smiles`. `smiles_to_ohe` then encodes the randomized string against that vocabulary and truncates with `.take(max_length)`; tokens outside the vocabulary silently produce an all-zero row.
consequence: Measured on 4,000 QM9 molecules with the pipeline's own tokenizer regex: 61.8% of randomized SMILES are longer in tokens than their own canonical form, and 0.2% exceed the longest canonical training SMILES, so those molecules lose their tail tokens entirely. The vocabulary itself is safe here — QM9 canonical SMILES use 29 distinct tokens against a --max_vocab default of 30 (process_and_train.py:310) — but the length ceiling is set by the wrong string. randomized_smiles is excluded from the ANOVA anyway (generate_paper_figures_v2.py:139, "Incomplete coverage"), which bounds the damage.
other_pipeline: No equivalent in KIRBy — the experimental pipeline has no SMILES one-hot representation to compare against.
source: Feature / representation identity on the QM9 pipeline (rust/src/main.rs + scripts/process_and_train.py), cross-checked against the experimental pipeline (KIRBy) and against paper.tex
evidence: Confirmed by reading: the one-hot vocabulary and maximum length are measured on CANONICAL SMILES even when the requested representation is randomized_smiles, and 61.8% of randomized SMILES are longer in tokens than their own canonical form. LATENT: randomized_smiles is in DROPPED_REPS and refused by name, so no run can reach it.

title: Two latent record-misalignment routes in the Rust writer, currently unreachable on QM9
what_the_code_does: (a) The Python writer emits `struct.pack("I", 0)` for a missing randomized SMILES (process_and_train.py:471) and the Python reader always consumes 4 bytes, but the Rust re-write path writes the length prefix only inside `if let Some(randomized) = &smiles_data.randomized_smiles` (1691) — so a record with no randomized SMILES comes out 4 bytes short. (b) `read_smiles_data` rejects any record whose isomeric SMILES is under 5 characters (1426-1430) after having already consumed that field, and `write_data`'s `if let Some(...)` (1631) then continues the loop from a mid-record offset with no error.
consequence: Neither fires on QM9 as configured: `split_qm9` skips molecules with no randomized SMILES (process_and_train.py:829-830), `Chem.MolToSmiles(..., doRandom=True)` always returns a string, and PyG's QM9 stores explicit-hydrogen SMILES so the shortest is '[H]O[H]' at 7 characters (verified by loading the dataset). Route (b) is live for the Polaris/MoleculeNet path (`load_and_split_polaris`), where ordinary SMILES such as 'C', 'CCO' are under five characters and would be dropped mid-record. Route (b) also aborts rather than corrupts when it hits a TRAINING record, because read_train_labels errors on a None (1530-1541); it is the val/test splits where it degrades silently until the leftover-bytes check fires.
other_pipeline: Not applicable — KIRBy holds features in memory as numpy arrays and has no packed record format to misalign.
source: Feature / representation identity on the QM9 pipeline (rust/src/main.rs + scripts/process_and_train.py), cross-checked against the experimental pipeline (KIRBy) and against paper.tex
evidence: Confirmed by reading; both routes need randomized_smiles, which is now refused by name in DROPPED_REPS, so neither is reachable. Route (b) -- a record rejected mid-read -- is the same fault as #64 and IS fixed: read_smiles_data panics rather than returning None mid-record.

title: The Rust writer omits the randomized_smiles field entirely when it is empty, while both readers always consume 4 bytes for it
what_the_code_does: Python's writer always emits the field when the rep is enabled: a 4-byte length plus bytes, or `struct.pack("I", 0)` for missing (process_and_train.py:466-471). Rust's reader always consumes the 4-byte length when the rep is enabled (main.rs:1441-1450), and leaves `randomized_smiles = None` when it is 0. But Rust's writer is `if let Some(randomized) = &smiles_data.randomized_smiles { ...write len, write bytes... }` (main.rs:1691) — for None it writes NOTHING, not even a zero length. parse_mmap unconditionally reads 4 bytes for the field (process_and_train.py:1162-1164). Also, the OHE block at main.rs:1750 does `smiles_data.randomized_smiles.as_ref().unwrap()`, which panics on the same input.
consequence: A single record with an empty randomized SMILES makes every following record in that file 4 bytes short of where the reader expects it, and the stream cannot resynchronise. It is currently inert on QM9 only because split_qm9 skips such molecules before writing (L829-830); nothing enforces that, and the Polaris/MoleculeNet path shares this writer.
source: QM9 data preprocessing and splitting (scripts/process_and_train.py, rust/src/main.rs)
evidence: Same latent route as #48(a): the Rust writer omits the randomized_smiles length prefix when the field is empty while both readers always consume 4 bytes. Unreachable while randomized_smiles is refused by name.

title: Provenance columns written by both pipelines are read by neither the figure script nor anything else
what_the_code_does: `grep -n "spec_version\|spec_hash\|gp_collapsed\|gp_fit_method\|params_source\|file_no\|temperature"` over the whole figure script returns no hits for any of them. `save_results` writes `spec_version`, `spec_hash`, `gp_fit_method` and `gp_collapsed` (utils.py:69-72); KIRBy writes `spec_version`, `spec_hash`, `gp_fit_method` plus 17 realised-dose columns (lines 1741-1762); `save_uncertainty_values` writes `file_no` and `temperature` (utils.py:266, 278/282).
consequence: Three concrete losses. (1) `gp_collapsed` marks a GP fit that predicted a constant — models.py:1878-1881 records it precisely so a failed fit is not read as a bad representation — but the figure script averages collapsed fits into auc_norm alongside real ones. (2) `spec_version`/`spec_hash` are never filtered on, and the model_defaults change log states that 1.1.0 'INVALIDATES every existing forest and quantile-forest result'; rows written under 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 are pooled and averaged by `calculate_robustness` with no guard. (3) `gp_fit_method` distinguishes the botorch fit from the Adam fallback, i.e. two different fits, also pooled.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back
evidence: Confirmed by grep: no hit for spec_version, spec_hash, gp_collapsed, gp_fit_method, params_source, file_no or temperature anywhere in the figure script. FIXED: generate_report now ends with a PROVENANCE ON THE ROWS section that prints the distinct values of each provenance column for the QM9 results, the QM9 uncertainty rows and the experimental results -- and WARNS when one frame mixes more than one spec_hash, or when any row came from a collapsed Gaussian-process fit. Executed on a fixture: both warnings fire.

title: Three docstrings describe behaviour the code does not have
what_the_code_does: `fix_injected_noise` says 'The saved injected_noise = y_true_noisy - y_true_original, but these are in different scales' — the writer at utils.py:252-257 has computed the linregress residual since before this reader was written, so the bug it claims to fix is not there. `load_validation_uncertainty` says the validation files are 'saved for the LEGACY (Gaussian) strategy only' and 'there is no per-sample injected_noise' — KIRBy line 1756 writes every condition under `--unc-conditions all`, and line 1841 writes a real per-sample `injected_noise`. `create_validation_uncertainty_table` repeats both claims and prints 'Gaussian strategy only' unconditionally at line 1315.
consequence: A reader checking whether the validation uncertainty table needs a condition filter is told, in the code, that it does not. That is what allows the pooling described in the finding above to look intentional.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back
evidence: Confirmed: the fix_injected_noise docstring described a bug that was never in the writer. All three notes corrected in place.

title: A dead conformal branch and an orphan partial file
what_the_code_does: `is_conformal = 'conformal' in model` gates a special coverage path, but `GLOBAL_MODELS_EXCLUDE` (line 118-121) lists conformal_rf, conformal_qrf, conformal_dnn and their _split variants, and they are dropped at load time (line 955-963), so the branch can never execute. Separately, KIRBy writes `all_results_partial.csv` after every fold (line 1852-1853) and never removes it or folds it into `all_results.csv`; `load_validation_data` reads only `all_results.csv` (line 1127), so the partial file persists as a same-schema file that no code reads.
consequence: No wrong number today. The conformal branch will mislead anyone who reinstates those models; the partial file is a plausible-looking results CSV sitting next to the real one, and its rows are a prefix of the real run, so hand-inspecting it gives a truncated picture.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back
evidence: Confirmed: GLOBAL_MODELS_EXCLUDE drops every conformal wrapper at load time, so the is_conformal branch cannot execute. Left in place with that written next to it rather than deleted -- it is the right handling if the conformal arm returns. The orphan all_results_partial.csv is the experimental runner's checkpoint and is deliberate.

title: Coverage and uncertainty-error correlation are pooled across every noise level on both sides
what_the_code_does: `model_data = rep_data[rep_data['model'] == model]` is every row for that model/rep across all 11 sigmas and all 10 iterations. `unc_err_corr`, `cov_1sigma`, `cov_2sigma` and `Mean Uncertainty` are then computed once over that whole stack. The validation mirror at line 1264-1290 does the same, grouping only by (dataset, model, rep) and pooling over sigma, over `noise_type`, and over `split`; its docstring at line 1252 even says 'Pooled across σ (matching the QM9 table)'.
consequence: One 'Coverage 1σ' number is reported for a quantity the shared spec documents as moving from 0.546 to 0.978 across noise levels (model_defaults.py, UNCERTAINTY_DEFAULTS comment). The single number is a weighted mean over the noise axis and is not the coverage of any condition that was actually run. This is an average over the very axis the study is about, and it is not disaggregated anywhere in table4.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back
evidence: Confirmed by reading: unc_err_corr, cov_1sigma, cov_2sigma and Mean Uncertainty are computed over every noise level and every replicate for a (model, rep) at once, and the validation mirror does the same. A coverage pooled across levels is not a coverage at any level. NOT FIXED -- computing them per level changes the SHAPE of table 4, which is the author's call. The report now says out loud what is pooled, so the number cannot be read as a per-level one by accident.

title: auc_norm is averaged across all six noise conditions and all representations for the headline cross-dataset figures
what_the_code_does: `model_ds_c = val_auc_df.pivot_table(values='auc_norm', index='model', columns='dataset', aggfunc='mean')`, `qm9_means_c = qm9_auc_df.groupby('model')['auc_norm'].mean()`, and `qm9_mn/ext_mn = ...groupby('model')['auc_norm'].mean()`. `auc_df` from `calculate_robustness` (line 1818) has one row per (model, rep, strategy), so `groupby('model').mean()` collapses 6 strategies × 5 reps into one number. The same pattern drives `compute_icc_and_redundancy` at line 2453 (`overall_auc = mean_auc.groupby(['model','rep'])['auc_norm'].mean()`).
consequence: Panel A and Panel B of the combined validation figure, and the model×dataset heatmap, report a robustness value no configuration has. Line 2453 is worse than cosmetic: the strategy-averaged correlations it produces are what justify `ANOVA_MODELS_EXCLUDE` (line 129-133, 'qrf: Redundant with rf (rho = 0.996)'), so a model is dropped from the ANOVA on the basis of an average across the six conditions.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back
evidence: Confirmed by reading: the cross-dataset bar and the transferability scatter average auc_norm over every noise condition AND every representation for a model, because calculate_robustness returns one row per (model, rep, condition). NOT FIXED -- whether the headline figure should be one condition, one representation, or the average is the paper's design. The report now names the pooling, and warn_if_axes_differ already names the axis mismatch (#96).

title: rmse, mae and the mean-uncertainty columns are in different units on the two sides while sharing names
what_the_code_does: KIRBy inverse-transforms neural predictions back to raw label units (`_to_raw`, line 952-954) and rescales the predictive std by `y_scale` (line 963), and trains tree models on raw `y` throughout; `compute_metrics` (line 1315-1326) then computes r2/rmse/mae in raw log units. QM9 standardises every label in Rust (`property_value = (property_value - mean) / std_dev`, rust/src/main.rs:1798-1799) and never inverts, so `calculate_regression_metrics` (utils.py:74-89) returns rmse/mae in standardised units and `save_uncertainty_values` stores `y_true_noisy`, `y_pred_mean` and the stds in standardised units.
consequence: `rmse` and `mae` mean different things in the two all-results files. More visibly, `table4_uncertainty_metrics.csv` reports 'Mean Uncertainty' and 'Mean |Error|' in label SDs while `table_validation_uncertainty.csv` reports them in log units, and the second table's docstring (line 1249-1256) says it 'Mirrors the QM9 uncertainty metrics'. Coverage, being dimensionless, is comparable; those two columns are not. The figure script's docstring at line 1181-1185 correctly notes the validation side is in raw units but nothing acts on the difference.
source: What reaches disk on both pipelines, and how the figure script reads it back
evidence: Confirmed: the experimental side reports rmse and mae in raw log units (predictions are inverse-transformed) while QM9 reports them on the standardised scale, under the same column names. Partly closed: standardisation_mean and standardisation_sd are now on every QM9 uncertainty row (#55), so the conversion is exact and recoverable. The results row does not carry them; putting the two pipelines' rmse in one table still needs the author to say which scale the table is in.
